source.title: What can be learnt with wide convolutional neural networks?
source.authors: Francesco Cagnetta; Alessandro Favero; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling affecting the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures generalization of wide convolutional kernels and compares convolutional with fully connected kernels on CIFAR-2, using kernel regression rather than the claim versions' standard training setups.
record.gate_note: Results about kernel learning curves, target structure, and CIFAR-2 kernel classifiers bear on V3. The paper does not test memorization of random labels, width beyond interpolation, optimizer or batch-size effects, dropout, magnitude-aware sharpness, or removal of memorized examples. The reported 53% versus 62% LeNet comparison is an architecture setup check, not a row for a listed version.
record.test_reason: The CIFAR-2 experiments compare held-out mean squared error of convolutional and fully connected neural tangent kernels, testing V3's architectural advantage through an infinite-width kernel method. They do not establish the result for finite networks trained with standard gradient methods.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The main conclusions concern infinite-width CNNs in the kernel regime: they adapt to localized target structure, but their random global outputs remain difficult to learn in high dimensions even with a Bayes-optimal matched student. The CIFAR-2 appendix separately reports that deep hierarchical convolutional kernels perform best among the architectures compared.
record.recipe_differences: Infinite-width NTK/RFK kernel regression with mean squared loss, rather than finite networks trained with standard gradient methods; synthetic teacher-student tasks and a CIFAR-2 regression experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Target spatial structure, kernel depth and filter sizes, input normalization, patch overlap, and noisy versus noiseless/regularized versus ridgeless settings affect the reported learning curves.

fits_no_version.finding: For synthetic regression targets supported on local groups of adjacent variables, hierarchical convolutional kernels have learning rates governed by target effective dimension; fully connected kernels remain governed by full input dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical convolutional kernels can exploit spatially localized target structure to improve sample-efficiency scaling over fully connected kernels.

fits_no_version.finding: Learning outputs of randomly initialized infinite-width hierarchical CNNs has an optimal error-decay exponent of 3/deff(L), which deteriorates with full input dimension.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hierarchical structure alone does not make random infinite-width CNN target functions efficiently learnable in high dimensions.

fits_no_version.finding: Modified LeNet without overlapping patches or pooling reaches 53% CIFAR-10 accuracy versus 62% for standard LeNet with the same hyperparameters.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing overlap and pooling together reduces accuracy in this LeNet comparison.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning; Proceedings of Machine Learning Research, volume 202, 2023.
record.problems: Most experiments are synthetic teacher-student kernel regression, not finite-network natural-label training. The CIFAR-2 comparison is figure-only in the supplied text and reports no numeric performance values; shaded empirical standard deviations are shown.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable reported outcomes exceeded the row cap. Synthetic learning curves were not entered as rows because the listed claim versions do not name their teacher-student target-structure outcomes.

untested.parts: Natural-label versus fixed-random-label training and held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond the width required for zero training error.

Finite networks trained from scratch with standard gradient methods; classification-error comparisons on the named benchmarks; isolation of local connectivity from other architectural differences; learned sparse local connections and convolutional initialization of fully connected networks.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons and tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Retraining after removing memorized versus random examples.

missing.what: Add the convolutional sides of the CIFAR-2 comparisons: C-NTK filter sizes (8,2) and (8,2,2), separately for each class pair. Their best-performance ranking is stated explicitly, although exact MSE values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
missing.locator: Appendix G.5 and final Figure S2, panels a–b, page 33

missing.what: Add shallow C-NTK with filter size (8) for each class pair. Appendix G.5 places shallow convolutional and fully connected architectures among the worst performers, qualifying any inference that convolution alone guarantees the observed advantage.
missing.locator: Appendix G.5 and final Figure S2, panels a–b

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains several figures numbered S2; the relevant CIFAR-2 figure is the final one on page 33. Its textual ranking supports qualitative states, but neither precise effect sizes nor statistical significance can be inferred. Shallow convolutional performance does not establish an absent or reversed CNN-versus-fully-connected effect because their pairwise ordering is not stated.

versions.untested_parts: No width sweep across the interpolation threshold.
Does not compare standard finite-width training; no MNIST, CIFAR-100, or SVHN comparison; no learned sparse local connections or convolutional initialization of a fully connected network.
No sharpness or generalization-gap measure comparison.
